title_en: Dialogue between a Montanist and an Orthodox Christian
author: Didymus the Blind
occasion: A literary dialogue defending the church's teaching against Montanist claims that Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla were inspired prophets and that the Paraclete had come in Montanus.
argument: The Montanist claims Paul's promise of 'the perfect' was fulfilled in Montanus as the Paraclete. The Orthodox speaker argues that 'the perfect' refers to the future vision of God face to face, when faith and partial knowledge will cease. He then shows from Scripture that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct persons sharing one nature, against Montanus's claim to be all three. He argues that the Spirit dwelt in the apostles and all believers as the pledge of promised goods, not that the apostles lacked the Spirit. Finally he argues that while women may prophesy, they may not teach or write books in their own name, which is why Priscilla and Maximilla are rejected as false prophetesses.

outline.move: The Montanist appeals to Paul's words about 'the perfect' coming, and the Orthodox speaker argues that this refers to the future face-to-face vision of God, when faith and partial knowledge will cease.

The Orthodox speaker shows that the apostles had the gift of prophecy, then quotes Montanus's claim to be Father, Son, and Paraclete, and argues from Christ's words that the Paraclete is 'another' distinct from Christ.

The dialogue continues on the Trinity, then turns to the apostles' possession of the Spirit, with the Orthodox speaker arguing that the Spirit dwelt in the apostles and all believers as the pledge of promised goods.

The discussion turns to women prophesying; the Orthodox speaker allows prophecy by women but forbids their writing books or teaching in church, and concludes that Priscilla and Maximilla are false prophetesses because they followed Montanus.

cast.name: Montanist
cast.who: An unnamed follower of Montanus who argues that Montanus was the Paraclete and that Priscilla and Maximilla were true prophetesses.

cast.name: Orthodox Christian
cast.who: An unnamed defender of the church's teaching who refutes the Montanist's claims.

cast.name: Montanus
cast.who: Founder of the Montanist movement, claimed by his followers to be the Paraclete; the Orthodox speaker calls him a false prophet and former priest of Apollo.

cast.name: Priscilla
cast.who: A Montanist prophetess whose writings are rejected by the Orthodox speaker.

cast.name: Maximilla
cast.who: A Montanist prophetess whose writings are rejected by the Orthodox speaker.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle, quoted extensively by both speakers.

cast.name: Mary
cast.who: The mother of Jesus, cited as an example of a woman who prophesied but did not have a gospel written in her own name.

cast.name: Philip
cast.who: The evangelist whose four daughters prophesied, cited as evidence that women may prophesy.

cast.name: Deborah
cast.who: An Old Testament prophetess cited by the Montanist.

cast.name: Miriam
cast.who: The sister of Aaron, cited as an Old Testament prophetess.

cast.name: Ananias
cast.who: Husband of Sapphira, who with her embezzled from the price of the field and was exposed by Peter's prophetic gift.

cast.name: Sapphira
cast.who: Wife of Ananias, who with him embezzled from the price of the field and was exposed by Peter's prophetic gift.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: The apostle who exposed Ananias and Sapphira.

cast.name: Abraham
cast.who: Patriarch whose two wives Paul interprets allegorically as the two covenants.

voices.speaker: Paul (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by phrases such as 'Paul says' or 'the apostle says', and by direct quotation of his epistles.

voices.speaker: Jesus (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by phrases such as 'the Lord says' or 'Christ says', and by direct quotation of the Gospels.

voices.speaker: Montanus (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by phrases such as 'Montanus says' and by direct quotation of his claim to be Father, Son, and Paraclete.

voices.speaker: Mary (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'the holy Mary prophesied, saying' (ἡ ἁγία Μαρία προεφήτευσε λέγουσα) and by direct quotation of the Magnificat; later referred to as 'the holy Theotokos Mary' (ἡ ἁγία Θεοτόκος Μαρία).

key_terms.sense: The Holy Spirit, the Comforter or Advocate promised by Christ; the Montanist wrongly identifies Montanus as the Paraclete.
The perfect or complete state that Paul says will come and do away with what is partial; the Orthodox speaker interprets it as the future vision of God.
What is partial: the present knowledge, prophecy, and faith that will cease when the perfect comes.
The distinct personal reality of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit within the one divine nature.
The Holy Spirit as the down payment or pledge of the good things God has promised.
A prophet, one who speaks God's words; the dialogue concerns whether prophets continued after Christ and whether Montanus and his followers were true prophets.
A false prophet, one who claims to speak for God but speaks against God's truth; applied to Montanus and his followers.
With uncovered head; the Orthodox speaker interprets this as a woman acting with authority and writing books in her own name, shaming her head, the man.
Head; in the discussion of women prophesying, the woman's head is her husband, whom she shames by acting with authority.
Allegorical interpretation; the Montanist objects to it, but the Orthodox speaker defends Paul's use of allegory to establish doctrine.
Fullness; the Montanist claims the apostles had only a pledge of the Spirit, not the fullness, which the Orthodox speaker denies.
Books written in the name of Priscilla and Maximilla; the Orthodox speaker says women may prophesy but not write books in their own name.

scripture: The author quotes the Septuagint and the Greek New Testament. Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint. Old Testament books are cited by their Greek names (e.g., 'the first of Kingdoms' for 1 Samuel). New Testament citations follow the standard Greek text. In a modern translation, cite as: 1 Corinthians, John, Matthew, Acts, etc., with standard modern chapter and verse.
uncertain: The exact date of composition of the dialogue.
Whether the dialogue reflects an actual encounter or is entirely a literary construction.
The precise identity of the 'Orthodox' speaker.
Whether the attribution to Didymus the Blind is original or secondary.

_unresolved_facts.fix: The source form is Πρίσκιλλαν (accusative), not Πρίσκιλλα (nominative). The nominative would be Πρίσκιλλα, but the source only shows the accusative form.
The source form is Μαξίμιλλαν (accusative), not Μαξίμιλλα (nominative). The nominative would be Μαξίμιλλα, but the source only shows the accusative form.
Jesus is not quoted in u01-rem-close. The sections should be ["u01-open", "u01-rem-early", "u01-rem-mid"].

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Μοντανὸς δὲ λέγει· Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ πατὴρ καὶ ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ υἱὸς καὶ ἐγὼ ὁ παράκλητος
_unresolved_facts.fix: Montanus is quoted in both u01-rem-early and u01-rem-mid. In u01-rem-mid: "Μοντανὸς δὲ λέγει· Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ πατὴρ καὶ ὁ υἱὸς καὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα" and earlier "Μοντανὸς ὁ τοῦ Ἀπόλλωνος ἱερεὺς ἀληθής" (ironic reference). Sections should be ["u01-rem-early", "u01-rem-mid"].
The source form is Φιλίππῳ (dative), but the nominative would be Φίλιππος. The brief should note the source shows the dative form, or include the nominative Φίλιππος as the standard name form.

The source actually reads "Μαρία ἡ ἀδελφὴ Ἀαρὼν" but the brief's identification as "Miriam" is an interpretation. The Greek name is Μαρία (Maria), not the Hebrew-derived "Miriam." The source_forms should be ["Μαρία ἡ ἀδελφὴ Ἀαρὼν"] and the name should be "Maria the sister of Aaron" or note that this is traditionally identified with Miriam.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Ananias ... who: 'Husband of Sapphira, who with her embezzled from the price of the field and was exposed by Peter's prophetic gift.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Πῶς γὰρ Πέτρος τὸν Ἀνανίαν καὶ τὴν Σαπφείραν ἤλεγξε νοσφισαμένους ἐκ τῆς τιμῆς τοῦ χωρίου, εἰ μὴ χάρισμα προφητείας εἶχε;
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says Peter exposed (ἤλεγξε) Ananias and Sapphira who embezzled (νοσφισαμένους), but it does not say Peter used a 'prophetic gift' to expose them—rather it asks rhetorically how Peter could have exposed them if he did not have the gift of prophecy (χάρισμα προφητείας). The 'who' should read: 'Husband of Sapphira; the source uses Peter's exposure of their embezzlement as evidence that Peter had the gift of prophecy.'

_unresolved_facts.claim: Sapphira ... who: 'Wife of Ananias, who with him embezzled from the price of the field and was exposed by Peter's prophetic gift.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Πῶς γὰρ Πέτρος τὸν Ἀνανίαν καὶ τὴν Σαπφείραν ἤλεγξε νοσφισαμένους ἐκ τῆς τιμῆς τοῦ χωρίου, εἰ μὴ χάρισμα προφητείας εἶχε;
_unresolved_facts.fix: Same issue as Ananias. The 'who' should read: 'Wife of Ananias; the source uses Peter's exposure of their embezzlement as evidence that Peter had the gift of prophecy.'

_unresolved_facts.claim: u01-rem-early move: 'The Orthodox speaker shows that the apostles had the gift of prophecy, then quotes Montanus's claim to be Father, Son, and Paraclete, and argues from Christ's words that the Paraclete is 'another' distinct from Christ.'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The outline omits that the Montanist first asks why they don't accept 'Montanus the holy' (Πῶς οὖν οὐ δέχεσθε Μοντανὸν τὸν ἅγιον;), and the Orthodox speaker's immediate response calling him a false prophet (ψευδοπροφήτης) and 'the abomination of desolation' (τὸ βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως). The exchange about the Trinity is preceded by this important characterization.

_unresolved_facts.claim: u01-rem-mid move: 'The dialogue continues on the Trinity, then turns to the apostles' possession of the Spirit...'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The section begins with continuation of Trinity discussion, but the turn to apostles' possession of the Spirit is specifically triggered by the Montanist's claim that the apostles only had an 'arrabon' (ἀῤῥαβῶνα) of the Spirit, not the fullness (πλήρωμα). The Orthodox speaker refutes this by showing the Spirit itself is the arrabon of promised goods. The outline should mention the arrabon/pledge concept as central to this section.

_unresolved_facts.claim: u01-rem-close move: 'The discussion turns to women prophesying; the Orthodox speaker allows prophecy by women but forbids their writing books or teaching in church, and concludes that Priscilla and Maximilla are false prophetesses because they followed Montanus.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Οὐ διὰ τοῦτο μόνον, ἀλλ' ὅτι καὶ ψευδοπροφήτιδες γεγόνασι μετὰ τοῦ ἐξάρχου αὐτῶν Μοντανοῦ
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Orthodox speaker gives TWO reasons for rejecting Priscilla and Maximilla: (1) they wrote books (implied by the preceding discussion about women writing books), AND (2) they became false prophetesses with their leader Montanus. The outline says 'because they followed Montanus' but should say 'both because they wrote books in their own name and because they became false prophetesses with Montanus.'

_unresolved_facts.claim: defending the church's teaching against Montanist claims that Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla were inspired prophets
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ψευδοπροφήτιδες γεγόνασι μετὰ τοῦ ἐξάρχου αὐτῶν Μοντανοῦ
_unresolved_facts.fix: The brief's 'inspired prophets' is too neutral. The source consistently calls Montanus a ψευδοπροφήτης (false prophet) and Priscilla and Maximilla ψευδοπροφήτιδες (false prophetesses). The occasion should say 'were true prophets' or 'were the Paraclete and true prophetesses' to reflect the Montanist claim being refuted.
